name: Confucianism
areas: Lu and the states of the Zhou
Confucius taught in Lu; his disciples and Mencius carried his teaching through the warring states
the learning of officials and the moral order of the state
its values are shared by hundreds of millions; few call it their religion
the state ideology of the Joseon kings
the orthodoxy of the Lê and Nguyễn kings
the official learning of the Tokugawa shoguns
Confucian temples and festivals in Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia
routes: With Han rule to the Red River delta
marks: Confucius was born in the state of Lu in 551 BCE, by the traditional date, and taught here; his temple and family cemetery are at Qufu.
Emperor Wu of Han set up official chairs for the Five Classics in 136 BCE and an imperial academy in 124 BCE.
The Temple of Literature, founded in 1070, became Vietnam's first national university (1076).
Zhu Xi revived this academy in 1179; his commentaries on the Four Books (1190) became the core of Neo-Confucianism.
The Sungkyunkwan, the Confucian academy of the Joseon kings, opened here in 1398.
The shogunate's Confucian temple and school at Yushima (1690).
The imperial examinations, based on the Confucian classics, were abolished in 1905.
notes: Confucius, born in the state of Lu (551 BCE by tradition), teaches that a good society rests on the virtues of its people and the rituals of family and state.
Confucius dies (479 BCE); his disciples gather his sayings, later compiled as the Analects.
Mencius teaches that human nature is good and that rulers who oppress the people lose the mandate of Heaven; Xunzi answers that it must be shaped by learning.
The Qin dynasty orders the burning of books (213 BCE), the Confucian classics among them, by the traditional account.
Emperor Wu of Han establishes official chairs for the Five Classics (136 BCE): Confucian learning becomes the training of officials.
After the fall of the Han (220), Buddhism and Daoism win many followers, but Confucian learning remains the language of government.
The Korean kingdom of Goguryeo founds a Confucian academy (372).
The Sui found the imperial examinations (605); Japan's Seventeen-article constitution (604) draws on Confucian ideals.
Neo-Confucian thinkers answer Buddhism; Vietnam founds the Temple of Literature (1070).
Zhu Xi publishes the Four Books with his commentaries (1190), the core of Neo-Confucianism.
The Yuan make Zhu Xi's commentaries the basis of the examinations (1313); in Korea the Joseon dynasty (1392) makes Neo-Confucianism its state ideology.
Vietnam's Lê dynasty (from 1428) makes Neo-Confucianism its orthodoxy.
Wang Yangming teaches the unity of knowing and acting; in Korea, Yi Hwang and Yi I debate Zhu Xi's philosophy.
Japan's Tokugawa shoguns adopt Neo-Confucianism as official learning; Confucian temples are built in Taiwan (1665).
The Qing emperors patronise Confucian scholarship and compile the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries (1773–1782).
Chinese emigrants carry Confucian temples and festivals to Southeast Asia; Japan's Meiji government turns to Western learning.
The Qing abolish the imperial examinations (1905); Confucianism is attacked as a cause of China's weakness after 1919 and again in the 1970s, and revived from the 1980s.
Few people claim Confucianism as their religion, but its values of family, learning and ritual are shared by hundreds of millions across East Asia.
src: Xinzhong Yao, An Introduction to Confucianism (2000)
